query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of aluminum (around 5 atomic %) into equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous and adherent Al2O3 scale without degrading its intrinsic room‐temperature ductility and high‐temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C (at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1), but with inadequate oxygen resistance due to the formation of non-protective oxide scales.
generation.intervention: Add ~5 at% aluminum (via alloying during melting/casting) to the original equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr composition, minimally perturbing the overall phase balance.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours; mechanical testing at room temperature for tensile ductility and at 1000 °C for yield strength under the same strain rate conditions as previously reported.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, continuous, and adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale on the surface of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum has a strong affinity for oxygen and, when present in small amounts, oxidizes preferentially to form a thermodynamically stable, slow-growing Al2O3 barrier that prevents rapid oxygen ingress (pesting). This protective scale limits further oxidation while the bulk alloy retains its desirable mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated equiatomic alloy, the Al-doped version will show a significantly lower mass gain and improved scale adherence during a 5-hour air exposure at 800 °C, with retention of the original room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (~163–530 MPa).
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy that suffers from rapid oxidation (pesting) under high-temperature air exposure with inadequate oxide protection.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable to cast refractory high-entropy alloys intended for applications involving air exposure around 800 °C for durations on the order of hours and where both room-temperature and high-temperature mechanical performance are critical.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum content and its potential subtle effects on phase stability and long-term mechanical behavior need experimental verification. It is uncertain whether 5 at% is ideal or if slight adjustments are necessary to balance oxidation resistance and mechanical performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the baseline equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and (2) an Al-doped variant with approximately 5 at% aluminum. Subject both sets to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours. After the exposure, assess the oxide scale formation via X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy, and measure mass gain (mg/cm2). Perform tensile tests at room temperature and yield strength tests at 1000 °C under comparable strain rate conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (i.e., similar mass gain and/or poor oxide adherence compared to the control) OR if the mechanical performance (tensile ductility or high-temperature yield strength) is degraded beyond acceptable limits relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: “Superalloy” is the general name given to iron-based, nickel-based, and cobalt-based alloys, given their high endurance, creep, and fatigue strength at high temperature. They are widely used in aviation, aerospace, and automotive and chemical industries, serving in high-temperature (≤ 1100 °C) environments. However, for super high temperature conditions of up to 1500 °C and 3000 °C, traditional surperalloys are powerless. Instead, a new type of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have shown their advantages. High-entropy alloys or multi-element alloys are loosely defined as solid-solution alloys that contain more than five principal elements in equal or near equal atomic percent (at%) [ [1] , [2] , [3] ]. HEAs usually have unexpected properties, such as high strength, high hardness, excellent softening resistance, and wear and corrosion resistance [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ]. According to the cocktail effects of HEAs, the alloy properties can be adjusted by composition changes and via alloying [ [4] , [5] , [10] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
